pointers.sentence: A fourth, `CSRF_SESSION_KEY`, `"_csrftoken"`, is the key the secret is kept under in a session (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CSRF_ALLOWED_CHARS`).
It is called in three places: by `get_token` when the request has none, by `process_request` when the cookie is malformed, and by `rotate_token` (`django/middleware/csrf.py:_add_new_csrf_cookie`).
Either way it masks the secret anew and returns the result (`django/middleware/csrf.py:get_token`).

`_unmask_cipher_token` splits a token at 32 and subtracts the mask's index from the cipher's; a difference below zero is used as it is, which a comment there calls fine: a negative index counts from the end of the string, and so comes to the same as modulo 62 (`django/middleware/csrf.py:_mask_cipher_secret`, `django/middleware/csrf.py:_unmask_cipher_token`).

`_unmask_cipher_token` splits a token at 32 and subtracts the mask's index from the cipher's; a difference below zero is used as it is, which a comment there calls fine: a negative index counts from the end of the string, and so comes to the same as modulo 62 (`django/middleware/csrf.py:_mask_cipher_secret`, `django/middleware/csrf.py:_unmask_cipher_token`).

Django's documentation gives the mask as protection against the BREACH attack: the field is scrambled differently in each response, and only the secret, not the token, is compared with the cookie's, so every token made from one secret is accepted (`docs/ref/csrf.txt`).
A value of 64 characters is unmasked, since, a comment says, Django before 4.0 masked the secret before storing it (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware._get_secret`).

A masked secret from before 4.0 is replaced only when the cookie is being sent anyway, as the comment there says: a post with such a cookie was accepted and set none, and the next page of the form set the 32 characters (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware.process_request`).

The comment gives the reason: other instances of `CsrfViewMiddleware`, as when a decorator and the middleware are both used, would otherwise set the cookie again; a `rotate_token` called after it, in another middleware's `process_response`, sets the flag again, and a later instance still honours it (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware.process_response`).

`CsrfViewMiddleware._set_csrf_cookie` sets the cookie with the secret and these settings, then adds `"Cookie"` to `"Vary"`, since, its comment says, the content varies with the cookie (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware._set_csrf_cookie`):
*The settings of the CSRF cookie, with their defaults from `django/conf/global_settings.py`.*

Django's documentation calls the cookie safe and the session common practice in other frameworks, and so sometimes demanded by auditors (`docs/ref/settings.txt`); keeping it out of the session by default lets a site protect the forms of visitors who have no session (`docs/ref/csrf.txt`).

The documentation calls the cookie the recommended source, and in a note recommends a masked token, against BREACH (`docs/howto/csrf.txt`).
The documentation says HttpOnly would give no practical protection: a script that can read the cookie already runs on the site's own domain (`docs/ref/settings.txt`).
`rotate_token` replaces the request's secret with a new one, flagged, so the response carries it and every token made from the old secret stops matching (`django/middleware/csrf.py:rotate_token`).

`login` and `alogin` in `django.contrib.auth` call it once the user is in the session ([The user of a request: `login`, `logout` and `AuthenticationMiddleware`](../auth/login.md)) (`django/contrib/auth/__init__.py:login`).
The documentation names the consequence: a form rendered before the login carries a token of the old secret and is refused, as after the back button or a login in another tab (`docs/ref/csrf.txt`).
